problems.statement: Core cause: a self-reinforcing workload loop in which vacancies drive agency use, agency use adds charge and orientation burden to permanent RNs (especially charge- and preceptor-qualified), burden drives resignations, and resignations drive further vacancies and agency use.

Pay erosion relative to the market (Larchmere scale up 3% a year against regional 9.4% and 7.9%, falling from 101% to 91% of median) is a real contributing cause of rising resignations and vacancies, but not the main one.

The presented explanation, that this is an external market problem and St. Brennan's poaching drives the agency bill, is largely rejected: resignations and vacancies rose steadily from 2024, well before St. Brennan's opened, and only 19 of 98 known leavers went there.

Agency spend growth is mostly a volume effect (about 77%, hours up 2.6x) and a smaller rate effect (about 23%) from the contract escalator tied to the wage index; the rate part is addressable through vendor renegotiation.
The 4 West pilot failed (CNO's reading) and shows the workload mechanism is wrong.

The 4 West pilot worked on the workload mechanism, since it removed exhaustion and the unit's resignations fell. The CNO's Q1 read was premature and confounded by leavers who had already given notice. Evidence is one unit, small counts, and short follow-up.

A sign-on bonus funded by suspending charge and preceptor differentials will worsen the loop. It adds new hires who need 12-week preceptorships while cutting pay for the staff who precept, and the 2025 bonus did not reduce vacancy or retain hires.
Insufficient hiring or slow time-to-hire is a main cause of vacancies.
Higher falls with injury on high-agency units are caused by agency staffing.

The vacancy and resignation trend began in 2024, before agency use rose sharply and before St. Brennan's. The pay gap and the loop probably both contribute to the initial trigger, and the origin of the loop is not fully identified.

causalClaims.from: Agency share on a unit rising
causalClaims.to: Charge and orientation shifts per permanent charge-qualified RN rising

causalClaims.from: Contract escalator tied to wage index
causalClaims.to: Agency rate increase (about 23% of the overrun)

causalClaims.from: Larchmere's pay falling behind the market

causalClaims.to: Lower resignations and exhaustion on 4 West

actions.action: Do not adopt the $15,000 bonus as designed (funded by suspending charge and preceptor differentials); hold it until the workload fix is under way.
actions.rationale: It cuts pay for the staff who must precept and orient the new hires, and the 2025 bonus raised hires only briefly while vacancy kept rising and 16 of 24 leavers left just after the clawback period.

actions.action: Extend the 4 West model (a nurse educator taking over agency orientation, a charge-shift cap backfilled by float charge RNs) to the 6 to 7 high-agency units, staged and measured against matched controls.
actions.rationale: It targets the verified loop, and 4 West resignations and exhaustion fell against matched units, so the cost is small beside the $18.9M spend.

actions.action: Retain, and consider raising, the charge and preceptor differentials; treat them as retention tools.
actions.rationale: Charge-qualified RNs are the most likely to leave (77% considering leaving), and they carry the orientation burden.

actions.action: Renegotiate or rebid the Vantage agency contract before its 2027-01-01 renewal, covering the escalator clause and the 6-8% lower competitor quotes.
actions.rationale: The rate effect is about $2.9M, and this saves money without touching the staffing loop.

actions.action: Consider a retention-focused pay adjustment toward the regional median for experienced RNs, funded outside the charge and preceptor differentials.
actions.rationale: The pay gap has widened to 91% of median and pay is a partial exit reason, but its size relative to workload is unproven.

actions.action: If a bonus is used at all, make it a smaller, retention-weighted award for existing staff and new hires, with a longer clawback or staged payments and with preceptor capacity secured first.
actions.rationale: Hold it until the workload fix shows results and the pay-versus-workload split is clearer.

actions.action: Reduce the buddy-orientation burden by lengthening agency assignments, using dedicated orientation staff, and reviewing the 13-week standard.
actions.rationale: Orienting a new traveler every week or two is the most common survey complaint (212 comments).

actions.action: Launch a recruitment campaign aimed at out-hiring St. Brennan's.
actions.rationale: St. Brennan's accounts for 19 of 98 known leavers, and hiring volume has not been the binding constraint.

actions.action: Act on the falls data as a staffing cause (for example by banning agency use on high-acuity units).
actions.rationale: The comparison is confounded by acuity and age and has no nurse-level linkage.

nextEvidence: Extended 4 West and matched-unit results over 3 to 4 more quarters, with leavers split by whether they gave notice before the pilot, and a pilot on a second unit.
Exit and stay interviews comparing the weight of pay against workload for charge- and preceptor-qualified RNs, and a cost model of differential changes against retention.
Unit-month analysis of falls adjusted for acuity, census and age, with nurse assignment recorded, and ATS data on candidate withdrawals by stage.
output.summary: The agency bill is mostly volume (77%), driven by a reinforcing loop. Vacancies bring agency staff, who add charge and orientation load to permanent RNs, which causes resignations and more vacancies. The lag analysis, exit interviews, survey and the 4 West pilot support this. The market and St. Brennan's story is weak: the trend began in 2024, and only 19 of 98 known leavers went there. Pay erosion contributes, and the contract escalator explains about 23% of the overrun. The proposed bonus, funded by cutting charge and preceptor differentials, would worsen the loop and repeat the 2025 result. Extend the 4 West model, keep the differentials, and rebid the agency contract.
